questions.statement: The bag is open, so I ___ the lid back in a second.
questions.context: A decision taken now, at the moment of speaking.

options.feedback: Correct! A spontaneous decision taken at the moment of speaking is expressed with will.
The present continuous would describe an arrangement fixed in advance, and this decision is being made right now.
The present perfect would claim the action is already finished, but the speaker is only about to do it.
The past continuous belongs to a past scene, and there is no past reference here.

questions.explanation:
Will carries several present-time meanings: willingness, a promise, a request and a decision taken on the spot. The open bag and the immediate reaction are the classic signal.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: We ___ to the coast next Saturday; we bought the tickets yesterday.
questions.context: The plan and the intention already existed before this moment.

options.feedback: Correct! A prior intention plus a fixed plan is expressed with be going to.
A bare present form would need a time clause, and here the trip is an intention rather than a timetable entry.
'Will' suggests the decision is being taken now, but the tickets show the plan already existed.
A present continuous for travel usually means an ongoing or imminent single trip, not a plan made in advance.

questions.explanation:
Be going to is the future of intention and evidence. Buying the tickets yesterday is the proof that the decision came before the moment of speaking.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The school bus ___ at seven in the morning, according to the timetable.
questions.context: A fixed timetable that belongs to the institution, not to the speaker.

options.feedback: Correct! Timetable events use the present simple with a future meaning.
A present continuous would turn the departure into a personal arrangement instead of a published schedule.
The future simple implies a decision taken now, but a timetable entry is already fixed.
This would suggest the speaker has a personal plan or visible evidence, which a printed timetable does not.

questions.explanation:
Fixed future events that are part of a public schedule take the present simple. The phrase according to the timetable is the reason.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: This time tomorrow we ___ across the border on the night bus.
questions.context: The action will be running at a certain moment in the future.

options.feedback: Correct! The future continuous describes an action in progress at a stated future time.
The bare present would make the trip a routine, not an event located at one future moment.
The future simple locates the action in the future without presenting it as already under way at that hour.
The future perfect needs a second reference point after the travelling is completed, which the sentence lacks.

questions.explanation:
This time tomorrow sets a single future point. The future continuous then places a continuous action at that point, and this is a common pattern in narrative and exam questions.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: By the end of the exam you ___ every reading text twice.
questions.context: The action will be finished before another future deadline.

options.feedback: Correct! By the end of plus a future point requires the future perfect.
The present perfect looks back from now, and the sentence is projected forward from today.
The future simple places the reading at or after the deadline instead of before it.
A present continuous cannot carry the projection to a future deadline.

questions.explanation:
By the end of the exam is a future deadline. What matters at that deadline is a completed action, so the future perfect will have plus participle is the required form.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: I promise I ___ the dishes before my sister comes home.
questions.context: A promise made in the present about a future obligation.

options.feedback: Correct! A promise given now about future action is expressed with will.
A present continuous would describe an arrangement already agreed, and no agreement has been announced.
'Would' belongs to conditionals and to polite requests, not to the flat promise the sentence announces.
The present perfect would claim the washing is already done, which contradicts the promise about what is still ahead.

questions.explanation:
Will is the tense of promises, offers and volunteer statements made at the moment of speaking. The contract here is between the speaker and the listener.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Do not touch the pan. It ___ not hot because the flame is still on.
questions.context: A negative prediction based on a present fact.

options.feedback: Correct! A negative prediction made at the moment of speaking uses will.
A passive present continuous would suggest the pan is being heated by someone right now, not a prediction.
The present perfect refers back to a past stretch of time and cannot carry the prediction.
The subjunctive were belongs to unreal situations and formal constructions, not to an ordinary prediction.

questions.explanation:
The warning plus the visible flame is a prediction drawn from present evidence at the moment of speaking. Will plus the adjective hot expresses the expectation.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Look at that dark cloud. It ___ rain, and we are going to cancel the match.
questions.context: Distinguish the two future forms in the same sentence.

options.feedback: Correct! The first clause is a prediction made now, so will is used, while the second states an existing intention.
Using be going to in the first clause would blur it with the intention reported in the second half of the sentence.
'Would' does not express a plain prediction about the immediate weather.
Shall is mainly used in offers and suggestions, not for predicting rain.

questions.explanation:
The same sentence can carry both future forms when they carry different meanings. The first half is a prediction and the second half an intention, and each clause keeps its own form.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The trip ___ on Friday afternoon; the flight is already booked.
questions.context: A future obligation based on an agreement already made.

options.feedback: Correct! A present continuous with a future time expression describes a fixed arrangement.
The present simple is for timetables and routines, and a personal booked trip is an arrangement instead.
The future simple would suggest a decision being taken at the moment of speaking, but the booking is already done.
The present perfect reports a departure that has happened, not one still ahead of us.

questions.explanation:
Arrangements have participants, a place and a time agreed in advance, so the present continuous is used. The booked flight is the evidence for that choice.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: We ___ meet at the corner at eight; I already told everyone the plan.
questions.context: The plan is definite and known to the listener.

options.feedback: Correct! A prior intention with an announced plan is expressed with be going to.
A present continuous would work for a scheduled arrangement, but the emphasis here is on the announced intention.
'Will' would make the meeting sound like a decision taken on the spot, which the announcement denies.
'Would' is conditional or polite, and it cannot report a definite plan.

questions.explanation:
I already told everyone signals that the decision is in place. When the intention and the information about it precede the moment of speaking, the future is be going to.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: By the time we reach the summit, we ___ the whole descent in record time.
questions.context: The completion of one action precedes another future action.

options.feedback: Correct! What matters before reaching the summit is a completed walk, so the future perfect is required.
The future simple leaves the walking open after the summit, so nothing is completed before the deadline.
The present perfect would place the completion before now rather than before a future point.
A present continuous would describe the walk as an ongoing arrangement, not as something finished by a deadline.

questions.explanation:
By the time is a future reference point and everything before it is looked at from there. The future perfect covers exactly that backward view from a future moment.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What ___ you going to do after the tournament?
questions.context: A question about a future plan, with the correct auxiliary.

options.feedback: Correct! The question keeps the present continuous because the question is about an existing intention.
Do cannot build the be going to form, which needs the auxiliary are or am.
A will question would ask about a decision taken now, not about the plan already formed.
Did belongs to the past simple and has no connection with a future intention.

questions.explanation:
In questions and negatives the auxiliary of be going to changes to am or are while going stays in the base form: what are you going to do, why are they not coming.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The ceremony ___ on the fifteenth at nine in the morning, according to the programme.
questions.context: A future event with a definite day and place, fixed by the organisation.

options.feedback: Correct! A published programme fixes the event, and will take place is the standard neutral way to announce it.
A present continuous would read as a personal arrangement, whereas the programme is an official announcement.
The present simple is the British norm for timetables, but with an exact programme a future form is the safer choice.
The present perfect would report an event that has already happened, while the programme still lists it ahead.

questions.explanation:
Take place is a useful phrase for events with a time and a venue. The future form in the announcement and the present simple in the British version are both defensible, and the programme settles it.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The phone has been ringing for a minute. Someone ___ be in the other room.
questions.context: A prediction about someone else's action, neutral in tone.

options.feedback: Correct! 'Must' expresses a deduction made from present evidence, and it is neutral in tone.
A will here would predict an action, while the sentence infers what is happening at this moment.
Can expresses possibility or ability and is far weaker than the certainty the evidence supports here.
'Should' carries advice or an expectation and is a weaker deduction than must.

questions.explanation:
Modal verbs for deduction rank by strength: must for certain, may for possibility, cannot for a rejected idea. The ringing phone is the evidence behind the inference.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Would you mind opening the window? No, ___ not, it is too cold.
questions.context: A refusal to accept a proposal made just now.

options.feedback: Correct! Will is the standard auxiliary for refusing an offer or request made in the present.
Did belongs to the past, and the offer is being made right now.
Do cannot carry a refusal on its own, and the sentence has no main verb without a modal.
A present continuous would be unusual here, and no form of be alone can answer the offer.

questions.explanation:
Will is also the modal of refusal. The contraction would not is built from the subject plus would plus not, and it closes an offer politely.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Shh. The baby ___ . Please close the door quietly.
questions.context: An action that begins now and continues for a period.

options.feedback: Correct! A present continuous describes an action happening at this moment.
The present simple describes a habit and would not explain the immediate request to be quiet.
The present perfect would report a completed sleep, but the baby is still asleep.
A future form is impossible here, since the request is about the situation in front of the speaker.

questions.explanation:
The present continuous is the tense of now. The imperative about the door confirms that the noise is happening at this exact moment, so the baby is sleeping.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: When you ___ the ticket, show it at the gate; they will not let you in without it.
questions.context: Two future events, one completed before the other begins.

options.feedback: Correct! A future time clause takes the present simple, and the print is the first step before entry.
This is the common error: a future form inside a when clause that refers to the future.
The present perfect would suggest the printing is already complete, but the ticket is still needed.
'Would' has no place in a neutral future time clause.

questions.explanation:
The main clause carries the future, so the when clause stays in the present. Print and then show is also a natural order of two future steps described in sequence.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: If you leave now, you ___ the closing ceremony.
questions.context: An expectation about a probable result.

options.feedback: Correct! A first conditional uses will for the open and likely future condition.
'Would' belongs to the second conditional, which describes an unreal or less likely situation.
A bare present after if could be read as a zero conditional about a rule, not as a future prediction.
The future perfect needs a later reference point, and the sentence has none.

questions.explanation:
The first conditional pairs a present condition with a probable future result: if plus present, will plus base verb. Leaving now is realistic, so the result is a real prediction.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: I ___ call the office right after this class and get you the dates.
questions.context: A spoken plan made during the conversation.

options.feedback: Correct! A decision taken during the conversation is expressed with will.
Be going to points to a plan formed earlier, and this call is being decided on the spot.
'Would' suggests a hypothetical or a polite offer rather than a firm on-the-spot decision.
The present perfect would claim the call is already behind us, which is the opposite of the intent.

questions.explanation:
The temporal phrase right after this class is the difference. A plan made now takes will, while a plan made earlier would take be going to.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: I usually work at home on Fridays, but this Friday I ___ from the office.
questions.context: An arrangement that has a habit-like quality for the speaker.

options.feedback: Correct! The contrast between the usual routine and the specific future moment is carried by the future continuous.
A present continuous would describe the present Friday or an arrangement, not the Friday that is still coming.
The future simple states the fact but loses the contrast with the ongoing routine the sentence opens with.
The present perfect continuous would need a present starting point, and this Friday is in the future.

questions.explanation: A future arrangement that stands out against a background routine is often expressed with the future continuous. The contrast between usually and this Friday justifies the choice.
questions.subject: ingles
